angleRead.name: Angela Reyes
angleRead.text: I'm standing at the pickup line outside the Rockridge school, and the story I want to chase is the one that doesn't look like a story at all. The table says Rockridge holds the strongest school record in the city — index 8.4, graduation 93.81%, college-ready 74.03%, teacher quality 9.12. But the number that moved this cycle is enrollment: Rockridge gained one student. Just one. And the index actually slipped from 8.46 to 8.4, which is the kind of thing I never write as a score moving because it didn't really move — it's the rounding of a stable table. What I want to chase is what that one new student means to the people who live it. The teachers on this slice — Maya Torres-Dillon, Rico Fiste

plan.interpretation: The stable quality table is the backdrop; the movement is in enrollment. Rockridge gained one student while the district added hundreds of employees — the story is in the mismatch between system growth and neighborhood stability, told through the people who notice a single new face in a classroom.
unverifiedLead: A mid-year enrollment often means a family moved for work or housing — the kind of detail I'd confirm with a principal before writing it.
The one-student gain could be a sibling joining an existing family, or a transfer from another neighborhood — worth asking, not assuming.
The district's 7.37% employee growth may mean more support staff, but it could also mean administrative growth — worth checking against classroom reality.
